title: Factorial Calculator
story: Your friend is studying combinatorics and keeps asking 'What's 5 factorial?' Instead of calculating 5×4×3×2×1 in your head every time, you build a function that computes any factorial instantly — even the big ones like 10!.
why: Factorial calculation with a while loop inside a function demonstrates accumulator patterns — keeping a running product that grows with each iteration.
analogy: Computing factorial is like stacking dominoes in a line and multiplying their values. You start with one domino (result=1). Each step, you pick up the next domino (i) and multiply it into the growing product. After n steps, you've multiplied all dominoes from 1 to n, and the final product is n!.
try_it: Calculate factorial(10) and factorial(0). Then write a `factorial_range(start: Int, end: Int)` function that prints the factorial of every number from start to end using your factorial function in a loop.
tips: Start `result` at 1 (not 0) — 0 multiplied by anything is still 0
Handle n < 0 as an edge case before the loop
The loop runs from 1 to n inclusive — use `<=` not `<`
factorial grows extremely fast — even 10! is already 3,628,800
common_mistakes: Starting result at 0 instead of 1 — every factorial would be 0
Starting the loop at 0 instead of 1 — multiplying by 0 ruins the product
Using an exclusive bound (i < n) instead of inclusive (i <= n) — misses the last multiplication
Forgetting to handle n < 0 — factorial is undefined for negative numbers
